source: But there is no turning back. Once you use the Book of Fates, the clock on Elsinore advances forever.
I can hardly believe this is true. Magic books? Godlike powers? What does any of it matter?
I just wanted to find a way to save them all-- and myself.
A perfect world is a notion held only by children and fools. And Ophelia, you are neither.
Here. This cursed thing is yours now. May you use it and find peace.
I have reason to believe Lady Simona is alive. Do you know anything about that name?
A Lady Simona? Can't say I do. There's an old hag by that name, comes 'round every week on Sundays. Pious, quiet woman.
She ought to be coming by this Sunday, in fact, later in the day. But she's no 'lady'. Couldn't imagine she'd be the woman you're searching for.
Irma thinks you need a firm hand to set you straight.
After all the grief I've given her lately, I cannot place blame with her.
All I can do is work harder to show everyone the man I wish to become.
Hmph. Is that so?
Well. I've a few choice words for that old maid Irma.
I'll find her on my own time, yes, on my own time...
Irma thinks Hamlet needs a 'firm hand' to set him straight.
I think Hamlet is his best self when he does that on his own.
And now that he's to be King, I have faith he will.
Not unless she wants to get a firm hand right back.
I don't think others understand the way a mind like his works. Not truly.
When someone is in the grip of such a despair, such a continual darkness... you cannot shake them from it by force.
Only love can dispel such a thing. And even then, it may take many years. Or he may never change at all.
Maybe. Something's changed in him as of late. He returned my lute, and...
Ophelia, do you think perhaps I've gotten Hamlet all wrong?
I'm starting to believe that things can be different between us.
Now that he's to be King, I don't know who would apply that hand to him.
Several firm hands, more like. And a swift kick in the rear for additional security.
So, Hamlet needs a firm hand?
He did. But now the boy is to rule. And I see some small thing is changed in him.
I once thought that boy could be King, before his father passed. And now I see it in him once more.
The seasons turn... and a youth becomes a man. So it goes.
Provided Hamlet treats me with dignity, I may bury my hatchet.
Truly, he's incorrigible. The boy must be stopped...
If not by me or my lady, then... who?
(And... that vial of poison shall lead the charge.)
(I knew it would prove itself useful.)
Irma thinks that Hamlet could use a firm hand to set him straight.
Oh, Irma. That's her way, I suppose.
Well. I should know her well enough. She did partially raise me, after all.
I wouldn't mind her. My son will soon go through a time of great change.
He hasn't had to rule before, Ophelia. He doesn't know how it alters you, moves through you.
Already I see something great changing within him.
Irma said that...?
I'll speak with her further. Thank you for telling me, Ophelia.
Irma thinks that Hamlet needs a good beating to set him straight.
I'm at a loss for what to do with the boy, truly.
I ought to show him a thing or two about how my father, his grandfather, tolerated a poor mood...
It involved the butt of a blade or the flat of his hand more often than not.
I know that your brother murdered you by pouring poison in your ear.
Then you know only one small piece of it.
I have suffered far more than anyone, even you, can understand.
Perhaps one year, one century from now—then you may come to comprehend.
Do you know anything about the strange vision I've been having? The one where all the castle dies?
You should know by now. Those are the events that were meant to come to pass.
That is the tragic fate which is written before you. For mine own self, it was my poisoning.
To think you can find a future where that does not happen is futile. Give up the sooner and you will drift into endless sleep.
I've never heard anything about Queen Astrid, King Hamlet's mother. What do you know?
Ahh, poor Astrid... She died young. I was in 'er service at the time.
Yeh know, she died in childbirth, but there were always those nasty lingering rumors...
Rumors of her death?
King Alexander wouldn't let anyone see the body, not even us guards, or the priest who'd bury her.
I'm sure 'e had his reasons, and grief is strange, but... there's always questions left over...
An' that mistress of his sure was beautiful. Simona, I think her name was.
Oh, look at me, prattlin' on about bones and dust. Excuse me, my lady!
Very little, I'm afraid. Her reign was before my time. Your father and Marcellus were both in service during those years. Perhaps they'd know more.
Your mother, Queen Astrid... I don't know anything about her. What was she like?
Ah... I haven't heard that name in quite some years.
She passed when I was but a boy, and my brother little less than. I never knew her well.
When we were young, courtiers often praised my brother Hamlet for how strongly he resembled our mother, with her fair features. I've never spoken to him about her death.
My father loved her deeply, in the time they were wedded. Then he, too, died, and it was just my brother Hamlet and I, stuck with one another.
Your father served Astrid greatly, as with my father. Now he provides me with his service. A family legacy, of sorts.
Brit. What do you know of King Hamlet's mother, Queen Astrid?
Astrid? That's awfully specific. Who wants to know?
Just me. Sheer curiosity.
My grandmother knew her well. She attended court when Astrid was growing up. They were about the same age.
And you've heard of her?
Hmph. Of course. Unlike some women here, my pedigree runs deep.
She didn't really die of childbirth, you know. That's just the nice story they tell.
What's the truth, then?
...I've simply got to laugh, 'Feely. Here you are asking me for answers when your dear ol' father's the biggest Astrid expert of us all.
I know nothing at all about Claudius's mother, Queen Astrid. Did you know her?
I... You know, I'm quite afraid I don't.
I arrived in Elsinore some years after her passing, at the behest of Hamlet's father, King Alexander.
By that time, she was already long dead. Then there was that stir with Alexander's mistress running off...
Just a moment. His mistress?
You mean Simona?
Oh, yes, Simona. She was known to the court, and was something of a favorite of his, at least that's what I heard when I was young. But then she up and vanished.
Most peculiar. I never did think to wonder why. You don't think about these things when you're a child.
Irma, you've been here a long time. What do you know about Queen Astrid?
Hrm! I may be old, but Gerta and I had not yet come to Elsinore then!
Still, looking at King Alexander, Claudius's father... I cannot understand how any woman survived marriage to such a man.
He had such a cruel manner to him. I often saw him cuff the boys across the backs of their heads. In public, no less.
And it's said he discarded her in favor of younger women quite often-- a womanizer who could not be satiated!
The rumor goes that lady Astrid lost her mind. Wouldn't any of us do the same with a man like that?
Or you'd kill him. One of the two!
Do you know much about Queen Astrid?
Ah ha... Queen Astrid and Lady Simona, two peas in a pod.
Both of them equally obnoxious, in the end.
I'll have to find a nice death for that Simona woman, in time.
You know, I've once spent entire game matches doing nothing but dismembering my opponent.
Though, to be quite honest, Lady is a mite of a stretch.
They were both little bosom pals with your mother, if memory serves. How is your mother doing?
She's dead.
Oh. Oh, dear. Terribly sorry. I suppose that's what happens when you pop out for a bit and come back. In two decades.
Your mother—Queen Astrid—What more can you tell me?
She passed when Claudius and I were both children.
Evidently, she died of childbirth with my brother. One more life he's ruined in this world, I expect.
It matters not. My father loved her, at least in front of the court, and I remember her very little.
Come to think of it, your father and your mother were both ardently devoted to her.
What do you know about Queen Astrid?
Ah. Now that's a name I'd sworn not to speak again.
Was there some ill omen about her death?
Your mother was wonderfully faithful to Queen Astrid during her service. She served her as a handmaiden, in the same way I advised King Alexander.
I...it's strange. I just came from visiting your mother's grave.
Thinking of your mother is... painful.
I wish you'd join me in visiting her too, now and then. We could pay our respects together. Perhaps then I could find the courage to talk about... what happened.
But now is not the time to unfurl feelings I've neatly tucked and folded away.
What happened to her, then? Why does no one speak of her?
I'm going to visit her grave, soon. Won't you come with me? Perhaps then I could find the courage to talk about... what happened.
I'm sure your mother would be smiling in Heaven, to think of you visiting.
Certainly, Father. I'll be there.
I found out what you did to my mother.
Your... mother?
Yes. When the plague came. Don't you remember?
Death is a wall. Very little permeates it.
Ah. Well, then. Allow me to refresh your memory.
You sent my mother, the only woman who looked after your mother in her final moments, the wife of your chief advisor, to her death.
When she was sick, you could have kept her in the castle. You could have had your servants bathe her with cool cloths, or bring her water when she vomited.
And at night, a fire if she shivered. Isn't that what all sufferers deserve? Compassion?
She might have survived, then. She might have made it.
But you didn't do that.
Instead, because she was not herself nobility, you ordered that she be sent to a sanitarium far from her family.
And she died, in pain, alone, far away from anyone she loved.
You're lying.
You do remember, don't you?
I am ashamed.
But I cannot hide the truth.
All I can do is offer my deepest apologies. My decision was clearly in error.
